activities.anchor: did not arrive in your mind like a video playing back
activities.caption: bet before you read on — the impossible patient
activities.name: memSkillPredict

config.q: A patient cannot form new conscious memories. Can they still master a new skill?
choices: No — without memory there is no learning
Yes — skill learning runs on separate machinery
Only if the skill is verbal
Only within the first hour of practice
config.why: Explicit filing and skill learning are separable systems — the lesson's deeper layers meet exactly that patient (H.M., mastering mirror-drawing day after day with no memory of ever practising).

activities.caption: file the three jobs of the memory system
activities.name: memJobBuckets

config.prompt: Encoding, storage or retrieval? File each job of the memory system:

items.label: translating light and sound into a form the system can keep
noting time, space and frequency with no effort at all
keeping the trace across months and years
reassembling the birthday scene just now
measuring how much comes back, how fast the decision, which errors appear

config.why: The processing cannot be watched — it is inferred from behaviour: how much is recalled, how fast a decision is made, which errors people make. Schemas shape every stage.

activities.anchor: Memory itself is not one thing
activities.caption: order the journey through the stores
activities.name: memChainOrder

config.prompt: The multi-store chain — order the journey of a memory:
items: A raw impression sits in the sensory store — a flash, an echo, gone in under a second
Attention selects what moves into working memory, the conscious workspace
Rehearsed or elaborated, it is filed into long-term memory — effectively unlimited
Later, retrieval rebuilds it from the archive into something that feels like playback
config.why: The multi-store model of Atkinson and Shiffrin (1968) remains the map on which almost every memory finding gets pinned.

activities.anchor: A memory is not a gift you have or lack
activities.caption: find the faulty line — an encoding briefing
activities.name: memEffortSpot

config.prompt: One line of this encoding briefing is wrong — click it:
lines: Automatic processing files away time, space and frequency with no effort at all.
Effortful processing demands attention and work — which is exactly why it can be helped or sabotaged by technique.
Some people simply have a good memory and some people a bad one, like a fixed camera quality.
Encoding strategy, retrieval practice and sleep vary enormously between people and dominate real-world performance.
config.correction: Memory is a set of processes, not a single talent — capacity is largely fixed and unremarkable in everyone; technique is what varies, and techniques can be taught.
config.why: The students who 'have good memories' are almost always running better techniques.

activities.caption: pair each component with its role
activities.name: memWmMatch

config.prompt: The working-memory model — pair each component with its role:

pairs.right: rehearses sound and speech — the inner voice
manipulates images and spatial layouts — the inner eye
the attention manager deciding what the two loops work on
binds the streams into single episodes handed to long-term memory

config.why: Which is why you can hum a tune while reading a map — different stores — but cannot read and hold a conversation: both compete for one.

config.prompt: The 2009 doodling experiment, step by step — order it:
items: Listen to a deliberately dull mock telephone message listing who would attend a party
One group shades printed shapes while listening; the other just listens
A surprise memory test on the names and places
Doodlers recall about 29% more — roughly 7.5 items versus 5.8 for the listeners
The mechanism: spare sketchpad capacity otherwise fills with daydreaming that competes with the message
config.why: Doodling occupies just enough of the sketchpad to block the daydream without overloading the loop — attention, not effort, is the bottleneck.

activities.caption: true or false — the doodling myth
activities.name: memDoodleJudge

statements.s: Doodling occupies an under-used store — the sketchpad — leaving the verbal loop free.
statements.why: The benefit is specific to tasks that tap a different subsystem.

statements.s: Doodling is multitasking that uses up the same attention as listening.
statements.why: It works because it occupies the under-used sketchpad; the verbal loop stays free.

statements.s: Genuinely competing verbal tasks, like texting while listening, impair recall badly.
statements.why: Unlike doodling, they compete for the same verbal resources.

statements.s: The doodling result is the central executive's lesson in action: attention, not effort, is the bottleneck.
statements.why: Exactly the working-memory model's executive doing its job.

activities.anchor: The two strongest fighters are well replicated
activities.caption: drag the divider — same hours, two schedules
activities.name: memSpacingCompare

config.prompt: The same three hours of study, two schedules — drag the divider.

before.label: massed: one three-hour block
before.text: Every encounter arrives while the trace is still fresh, so retrieval takes little effort — and a comfortable feeling of familiarity does the talking.

after.label: spaced: three one-hour sessions across a week
after.text: Each new encounter arrives when the trace has partly decayed — the extra effort to retrieve it strengthens the trace more.

config.why: The spacing effect, one of psychology's most reliable findings — and it compounds with its fellows: retrieval practice, sleep (consolidation), chunking and mnemonics, and the self-reference effect.
